title: Bodhisattva Vows 2
speaker: Yuzan Nancy Welch
summary: Yuzan Nancy Welch shares that taking Bodhisattva vows literally can lead to feelings of inadequacy, but instead suggests cultivating awareness and intention by embracing a mindful and compassionate approach. This means recognizing the Buddha nature already present within themselves and others, rather than striving for perfection. By doing so, they encourage listeners to focus on serving others and using their energy to help them find their own path to happiness, rather than indulging in personal gain or comfort.

sentences.text: Well, tonight I'm going to speak about the last two of the great bodhisattva vows: entering boundless gates and becoming what cannot be surpassed.
In the verses: *Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.* As John discussed so well last week regarding the first two of these vows, these vows are enormous.
Impossible if taken literally.
So how can we commit ourselves to doing what is implied in the vows themselves?
Impossible.

How do we reconcile our desire to save all beings and all delusions and understand and be the living limitless dharma, ultimately attaining the enlightenment of Buddha, when they're telling us it's impossible?

I had been practicing Zen for three or four years, repeating the vows along with everyone else at the appropriate times, just like I recited the prayers and responses expected during the bazillions of Catholic Masses I attended growing up.
We had to go to Mass every day during the school year.
And just like that experience of simply memorizing and repeating, I had been saying the Bodhisattva vows by rote for some time.
But at the close of just a random day of our summer sesshin at Samish some years ago, I actually heard what I was saying.
And the enormity of this massive chasm that I felt between what I was saying and how I was practicing, how I actually wanted to be living my life, hit me, really hit me in the gut like a wham.
I couldn't even finish the vows.
I couldn't finish reciting them with everyone.
I just started sobbing, and it was the end of the day, and as everyone filed out of the zendo, I sat back on my cushion and I just cried and cried.
I felt devastated, sickened by the certainty that I had failed.
I would continue to fail, and I had gotten caught not just in taking the words literally at that moment but, more overwhelming, in the desire I felt suddenly to fulfill those vows, to be that Buddha.
And if I couldn't do it, well, how worthless could I get?
I know this sounds very melodramatic, but this is what happened that evening.
I was consumed with the delusion that I should be that Buddha, and I never would, and I felt my heart break.
Well, after I scraped myself off the Zabuton and sniffled back to my cabin, I did not have sudden enlightenment.
I did realize, however, that I was indulging in two very familiar paths of thinking for me: the striving for perfectionism and then the self-pity that ultimately follows that.

So this talk is really a very good talk for me to give, as I have had to revisit that evening, which I hadn't thought of in some time, and consider how my understanding of the Bodhisattva vows has changed and continues to change with the study of the Dharma.
Last week John gave us the definition of vow, I believe.
I would like to offer a sort of companion definition of the word intention.

Before we recite the vows there is an introductory piece that says *may our intentions equally penetrate every being in place with the true merit of Buddha's way.* The word intentions, I believe that concept, I'm sorry, I believe that concept is instrumental in how to practice with the great vows.

Webster's dictionary defines intentions as *purpose or attitude as to the effect of one's action or conduct on others or events.* Applied to the vow *Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them,* Reb Anderson explains in his book Being Upright that though we say enter, we vow to enter the gates.
The Chinese character in that vow literally means to learn or to understand.
To learn or to understand is not only directed towards studying the written words of Buddha's teachings, the massive amounts of doctrine that intimidate me.

Reb states that in practicing the third great vow we recognize that everything that comes to us is the gateway to the truth, and we vow to use every meeting with every other living being or thing as an opportunity for realizing the truth.
At the same time there is no demand to enter all possible gates, to force the creation of those opportunities, but only to recognize them and respond to them as they present themselves.

I found a Buddhist internet site called the awakened teachers forum, and they had a discussion of the third vow, all the vows actually, and what I read was that the third vow also encompasses the practice of skillful means.
It cites examples of how Buddha suggested different practices for those who sought his help, depending on their individual needs.
For one person he might emphasize, I guess it's Pali, Samatha or Shikantaza, just sitting practice.

For another he might demonstrate that transmission of the Dharma could be found outside the doctrine, as in the case of, you know who I'm talking about, [unclear: "Mahakapastha"]'s smile: when Buddha held up the flower, he smiled and understood and was enlightened.
Gil Fronsdale, a Soto Zen and Vipassana teacher and a student of Jack Kornfield, sees the third great vow as corresponding to both the third and the fourth noble truth.
The boundless Dharma gates offer multiple ways out of the truth of suffering and the causes of our suffering.

Buddha offers the eightfold path as a guide away from suffering, but the boundlessness of the Dharma gates actually allows for myriad ways to find freedom from attachment and aversion, the root of our suffering.

The fourth great vow, Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it, is the one that truly had me sobbing on my cushion that night of great delusion and self-pity, believing that I had to become the Buddha before I could be a Buddha.
I was not realizing the Buddha nature that was already in me, that's in everyone in every place.
Instead I put myself outside the realm of reality, refusing to see that I was already there.
The fear of not being good enough, I turned my concern inward on myself rather than outward towards others, and that's how one really suffers.

In the book John mentioned last week, Realizing the Genjokoan by Shohaku Okumura, I took out a piece that I think really related to this experience I had and helps me in my continuing understanding of the vows.
Okumura says:
*According to Dogen Zenji, attaining a one-time enlightenment experience in which we suddenly recover our Buddha nature is not the goal of practice.
Practice for Dogen is an ongoing activity in which we continue to deepen and broaden our understanding day by day, moment after moment.
For him, enlightenment is a vital life activity that we must nurture just as we nurture our bodies.
To stay alive we must eat, digest the food we've eaten every day, and we need to breathe moment by moment.
In the same way, to manifest awakening we must continually return to awakening day after day, moment by moment.
Whenever we find that we have strayed away from the path, we must return to it in our practice.
And our Zazen practice is Bodhisattva practice, and it is therefore the foundation of the four Bodhisattva vows.
The Bodhisattva vows are the basis for our practice outside the zendo as well as in.
It is an active, daily, moment by moment practice.
When we begin to practice with the four Bodhisattva vows, sooner or later we will see the incompleteness of our practice or notice that we have deviated from the Bodhisattva path.
Just as we return to our posture in Zazen as we begin to slump, we practice repentance by returning to the path of the Bodhisattva vows.
Whether in the zendo or going about our daily routine, moment by moment we simply return to awakening in genuine practice.
This we must do over and over again.
Our practice is endless.*
In the same book by Reb Anderson that I mentioned, Being Upright, Reb writes that this vow, the fourth vow, can also be expressed as Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to manifest it.

Manifesting Buddha's way is allowing our own Buddha nature to always be at the ready: practicing maintaining our awareness outward towards others, so that when the opportunity to help others, to learn from others, excuse me, so that when the opportunity to help others and learn from others arises, we're ready to engage.
In this vow I am especially aware of the meaning of the word intention.
Maintaining the awareness of the effects of my action on others is critical to stay on the path.
Again from the awakened teachers forum, there's a story that tells of three people traveling in a desert and dying of hunger and thirst.
They suddenly come upon a wall, look over it and see a paradise of food and drink and cool shade.
Two of them rejoice and leap over that wall into that wonderful place and ameliorate their hunger and their thirst.
The third person also rejoices and turns back to the desert to help others find the way to that paradise.
And that is one of the best ways I can think of to manifest the Buddha way.
Thank you.
